messages:
maya: Quick follow-up from the kernel-selection RFC — posting a compact proposal for a runtime seqlen scheduler + warmup heuristics. Looking for concrete objections before I turn this into a small PR.

alex: SG. Can you summarize the core change?

maya: tl;dr: move from a single global bucket table to a small number of dynamic buckets per-model that are driven by recent prefix length distribution, plus a short warmup trial for cold workers to calibrate kernel choice. Goals: reduce tail latency for mixed-length traffic and avoid bad kernel picks on cold starts. :thinking_face:

jorge: How many buckets are you thinking? previous RFC had like 8 fixed bins which caused fragmentation.

maya: propose 4 adaptive buckets: short, medium, long, jumbo. Boundaries are set via recent quantiles (10th, 50th, 95th). We keep buckets compact to avoid explosion in compiled kernels.

li: That sounds reasonable. How do we prevent thrashing if traffic shifts quickly (e.g., sudden long prompts)?

maya: two mitigations: (1) smoothing on quantiles (exponential decay with a 30s half-life), (2) for any bucket with less than N_samples (configurable, default 50) we prefer a conservative kernel (memory-safe slower path) until warmup trials complete.

alex: Warmup trials — concrete mechanism? do we just run a micro-batch on each new worker?

maya: yes, but controlled: when a worker first comes online or gets a bucket with low samples, it will run up to M trial requests sampled from in-flight requests (M default 8) using a shadow path that collects latency and peak-RSS. Trials are staggered so we don't blow steady throughput. If a trial shows the optimized kernel meets the latency tail and memory bound, we mark the bucket "hot" and enable it.

sam: Any impact on cost due to extra trials?

maya: small and bounded. Trials only occur at low-sample states or cold worker starts. We throttle to 1 trial per X seconds per worker. Empirically in staging this added ~0.3% token cost but reduced P95 by ~8% on mixed workloads. (bench numbers below)

jorge: Can we see the bench numbers you mentioned?

maya: pasted quick results from last run: 

```
workload: mixed(10%, 40%, 40%, 10%) short/med/long/jumbo
baseline (fixed 8 bins, no warmup): P50=12ms P95=174ms P99=410ms cost-index=1.00
proposal (4 adapt buckets + warmup): P50=11ms P95=161ms P99=392ms cost-index=1.003
notes: fused-attn kernels favored in short buckets; for jumbo we pick memory-frugal kernels (tensor-split)
```

li: Good. A few operational questions: how do we persist bucket info across restarts and rolling deploys? Don't want every worker to re-run warmup and flood requests with trials.

maya: bucket summaries are stored in the control-plane compact cache per model-version (keyed by model+variant). We store quantile estimates and last-hot-timestamp. Workers consult the control plane on start and only run trials if the bucket is not hot or last-hot is older than TTL (default 10m).

alex: What about KV cache implications? If we route by bucket, we might split requests across workers and miss cache hits for conversational sessions.

maya: good catch. We prefer session-affinity: routing policy keeps sessions on the same worker when possible. If a session extends into a different bucket (longer prompt), we allow a one-time migration with KV prefetch: worker A ships KV snapshot to B asynchronously and B runs a single catch-up warmup request for the session. If prefetch fails, fallback is to compute cold keys (slower).

jorge: Shipping KV snapshots across machines sounds heavy. What's the expected size?

maya: for typical chat workloads KV size is small (tens to a few hundred KB). We compress with a simple codec and cap transfers to 2MB. We also rate-limit cross-worker KV moves.

li: Eviction policy for cached buckets/kernels? JIT compile explosion is a real risk if models have many variants.

maya: eviction policy: global LRU on compiled kernels with per-model min-reservation (configurable). Also we avoid compiling for rare buckets: we only compile when a bucket exceeds compile_threshold samples in the aggregate.

sam: How configurable will this be in the console? Ops will want knobs for trial budget, bucket count, TTLs, compile thresholds.

maya: yep, expose under model config:

```
seqlen_scheduler:
  bucket_count: 4
  sample_decay_half_life_s: 30
  compile_threshold: 50
  trial_budget_per_worker: 8
  trial_throttle_s: 60
  hot_ttl_s: 600
  kv_prefetch_enabled: true
```

alex: One last thought: kernel selection cost model should consider memory-bandwidth and single-thread perf, not just flops. We should record microbenchmarks per-device (best-kernel-per-bucket table) and surface that to the scheduler so it doesn't select a kernel that's compute-heavy but memory-bound on particular GPUs.

maya: agreed. plan is to maintain per-device kernel profiles in control plane and weight trial selection using predicted mem-bandwidth headroom. Will add that to the PR.

infra-bot: deploy-check: staging config applied to pool "canary-runtime" — 3 workers will exercise warmup for the next 12 hours.

alex: cool, please add the small state-machine diagram and the PR link when ready. :thumbsup:

maya: will do. Thanks all — unless anyone objects, I'll open the PR tomorrow with a minimal opt-in flag.

jorge: no objections from me.

li: +1

sam: +1

maya: (closing) filed: https://git.internal/redwood/runtime/pulls/1429 — contains scheduler code + tests + a couple of lightweight perf scripts.
